articles.author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya, Turkey
articles.description:
Its key temperature goal has been missed but experts say the agreement is still proving a vital moral compass for progress
It was a curious way of conducting negotiations. Ahead of the 2025 climate summit, in the Amazonian port of Belém last year, the Brazilian hosts had taken off the table the issue that most had assumed would be at its heart: concrete plans from each country laying out exactly what they would be doing to cut their greenhouse gas emissions.
Brazil was insisting, instead, that these plans – the bedrock of the Paris agreement – were the business of national governments and not up for negotiation. “In that case, it will be a very short Cop,” one seasoned global south negotiator told the Guardian shortly before, reflecting a widespread unease. “There is nothing to negotiate.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
The president’s announcement comes days after an earlier attack on Iran was made public, and as diplomatic efforts to end the conflict have accelerated
Donald Trump has said the US military on Friday carried out a new round of limited strikes on Iran, targeting an air defence system, describing the action as “minor.”
Iranian state media reported the sound of two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, which is in the strait of Hormuz, the crucial waterway for oil shipments that has been disrupted since the beginning of the US war on Iran in February.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US carries out another round of ‘minor’ strikes on Iran, Trump says

articles.author: Robert Mackey, Shrai Popat, Anna Betts, Taz Ali and Adam Fulton
articles.description:
This live blog is now closed.

Stephen Miller, architect of Trump’s immigration crackdown, to become White House chief of staff

Sign up for Breaking News US email

Donald Trump will begin the day in Washington today. 
He has closed door meetings for much of the day, and will take part in a Diwali celebration at the White House at 1:30pm ET. While that’s currently not open to the press we’ll let you know if that opens up.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Democrats blast Trump’s decision to make Stephen Miller his chief of staff as president defends picking loyal ‘MVP’ - as it happened

articles.author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
articles.description:
Santiago Peña was detained minutes after he was impeached by Congress, as protesters took to the streets demanding answers after the suspension of the Ueno bank
Paraguay’s rightwing president has been placed under house arrest minutes after he was impeached by Congress, amid a severe crisis that left more than half the country’s population unable to access their bank accounts.
Santiago Peña is being investigated about allegations he used his political influence to favour a bank that expanded exponentially under his government and was suspended this week after irregularities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ousted Paraguay president under house arrest after banking crisis leaves 60% of country unable to access accounts

articles.author: David Smith in Washington
articles.description:
US president confirms Susie Wiles, current chief of staff and first woman to serve in the role, will step down

US politics live – latest updates

Stephen Miller, Donald Trump’s most controversial aide and the architect of his sweeping immigration crackdown, will become his new White House chief of staff days after Republicans lost control of the US Congress in US midterm elections.
The president announced the extraordinary appointment on Friday, confirming that Susie Wiles – his current chief of staff, and the first woman to serve in the role – had been ousted.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Stephen Miller, architect of Trump’s immigration crackdown, to become White House chief of staff

articles.author: Maanvi Singh
articles.description:
US voters repudiated mass deportation campaign, but choice of new chief of staff shows Trump doesn’t care
On Tuesday, voters resoundingly rebuked Donald Trump and his brutal mass deportation campaign that sent military tanks and masked agents though residential streets.
But on Friday, the president doubled down. He named Stephen Miller – the architect of the administration’s most aggressive immigration policies – as his chief of staff.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How Stephen Miller appointment shows Trump hasn’t learned his lesson on immigration

articles.author: Josh Butler
articles.description:
Zero Limits supplements is co-owned by rightwing podcaster and fitness coach Chris Katelaris, also known as ‘Big Chocky’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Ben Roberts-Smith has collaborated with a gym supplements company run by a rightwing influencer which recently sold a pre-workout product called “war crimes”. 
Roberts-Smith, one of Australia’s most decorated living soldiers who is currently awaiting trial on war crimes charges, has recently launched an apparel brand, Epic 1 Two, producing T-shirts and gym wear.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Ben Roberts-Smith collaborates with gym business run by influencer that sold ‘war crimes’ pre-workout supplement

articles.author: Associated Press
articles.description:
Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos arrested by secret service after telling officers voices told him to kill Donald Trump
The US secret service said a suspect has been taken into custody and charged after officers found him in a vehicle near the White House with multiple guns, claiming he heard voices in his head telling him to kill Donald Trump.
The arrest Thursday night happened after secret service officers approached a man “acting suspicious” in a parked car, according to a Homeland Security statement. US officials said the suspect – Ronny Yordrix Guanipa Chrinos – went on to describe voices in his head that were telling him to come to the nation’s capital and kill the Republican president.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Man in custody after being found in vehicle near White House with guns

articles.author: Vikram Dodd and Emine Sinmaz
articles.description:
Met police chief says ‘many more’ victims could come forward, as actor and comedian awaits sentencing 
Police are bracing themselves for more victims of Russell Brand to come forward, with at least 10 more women suspected of having been attacked by the disgraced star.
Brand, 51, will be sentenced on Monday to what is expected to be a lengthy jail sentence for rape and sexual assaults after he abused his fame to become a “predator” targeting women, and got away with it for years.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women

articles.author: Caitlin Cassidy
articles.description:
Primary school students bested 200,000 competitors across New South Wales to reach the Premier’s Spelling Bee finals in Sydney

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Competing in a spelling bee is not for the faint of heart. Sometimes, the difference between victory and loss is one incorrect vowel and you’re undone, months of training reduced to nought.
At a small theatre hall in Sydney’s west on Friday afternoon, 34 primary school students sit stony-faced on a brightly lit stage, knowing this pressure only too well.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: When a single vowel stands in the path to victory, the stakes could not be higher for these spelling bee champions

articles.author: Maya Yang
articles.description:
Wiles thanks president for ‘honor of a lifetime’ as departure leaves behind overwhelmingly male leadership team

US politics live – latest updates

Donald Trump on Friday said Susie Wiles, the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff, will leave her post, a major shake-up of his inner circle that comes amid a steady exodus of senior female officials from his administration.
The president announced her ouster – and her replacement, by the immigration hardliner Stephen Miller – in a post on Truth Social, days after a sweeping blue wave gave Democrats control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections. Wiles’s departure leaves behind an overwhelmingly male leadership team.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Susie Wiles exits White House as Trump ousts another woman from key role

articles.author: Richard Luscombe in Miami and agencies
articles.description:
Father of the Duchess of Sussex was taken into custody near Tampa, US prosecutors said
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested by US federal agents in Florida on Friday and charged in connection with possession of child sexual abuse material, according to the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI).
Markle, 82, was taken into custody at a senior care facility in Polk county early on Friday, and made a brief initial appearance in federal court in Tampa on Friday afternoon, the Associated Press reported. He was later released with the condition that he be electronically monitored.
In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453 or visit their website for more resources and to report child abuse or DM for help. For adult survivors of child abuse, help is available at ascasupport.org. In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found at Child Helplines International
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Thomas Markle, Meghan’s father, charged in Florida in connection to child sexual abuse material

articles.author: Mark Sweney and Graeme Wearden
articles.description:
Asian and European markets follow US tech rout with many analysts predicting more waves of selling to come
European and Asian stock markets fell sharply on Friday after the Democrats’ decisive victory in the midterms triggered a rout in US tech stocks a day earlier.
A sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday was followed by sharp falls in Asian stock markets on Friday. The investor sentiment then reached London, where the market was, at one stage, poised for its worst day since March.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Global stocks fall amid ‘big worries over AI’ after Democrats’ midterms triumph

articles.author: Johana Bhuiyan
articles.description:
Men allegedly impersonated voices and images of executives to convince employees to send large payments
Three foreign nationals were arrested and charged with using AI to allegedly impersonate corporate CEOs and attorneys to steal over $100m, according to an indictment that was newly unsealed by the US Department of Justice.
According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men – Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit – were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Three men charged in US with using AI to impersonate CEOs and steal millions

articles.author: Emine Sinmaz
articles.description:
Ian Winter KC told Rosamund Urwin of the Sunday Times, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward: ‘I hope you are pleased with yourself’
Russell Brand’s barrister has reported himself to his professional regulator after being accused of launching a tirade at a journalist shortly after his client had been found guilty of rape.
Ian Winter KC “confronted” the Sunday Times journalist Rosamund Urwin, whose investigation led to Brand’s victims coming forward, telling her: “I hope you are pleased with yourself.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russell Brand barrister reports himself to watchdog over clash with journalist

articles.author: Benjamin Lee
articles.description:
The Chilean film-maker, whose films starred Florence Pugh, Julianne Moore and Rachel Weisz, died at his home in Santiago
Chilean film-maker Sebastián Lelio has died at the age of 52.
He was best known for the Oscar-winning trans drama A Fantastic Woman and his English-language films included Gloria Bell and The Wonder.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sebastián Lelio, director of A Fantastic Woman and Gloria, dies aged 52

articles.author: Ian Sample Science editor
articles.description:
The most enjoyable conversations strike a balance between exploring a topic and pulling in fresh ideas, study finds
As an early stab at rules for conversation, Cicero did a fine job: watch your tone, never look bored, never lose your temper and never ramble on, particularly about yourself, he advised.
Now scientists have followed in the great orator’s footsteps and discovered a telltale signature of an enjoyable chinwag. The secret of a mutually satisfying exchange is a healthy dose of pink noise, they say.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is ‘pink noise’

articles.author: Ajit Niranjan
articles.description:
Separate actions also take place outside fence and across Europe in backlash against impact of AI boom
Activists have stormed the site of a Microsoft datacentre being built in Amsterdam, as the backlash to the social and environmental harms of the AI boom spreads across Europe.
Protesters from Geef Tegengas, a Dutch direct action group, clashed with police while breaking into a construction site at Westpoort, Amsterdam, where some members climbed a crane, lit flares and tied helium balloons to equipment.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Activists break into building site of Microsoft datacentre in Amsterdam

articles.author: Rory Carroll in Dublin and Jakub Krupa
articles.description:
Media organisations in Ireland and UK also affected as apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos continues
A fresh wave of bomb threats disrupted air traffic across Europe on Friday but the affected aircraft landed safely and searches revealed no explosive devices.
The latest alerts affected at least 18 flights to or from Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the UK.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Further bomb threats disrupt at least another 18 flights across Europe

articles.author: Jakub Krupa
articles.description:
This blog is now closed, you can read more on this story here
A Romanian airline Tarom flight from Prague to Bucharest is the latest believed to be affected by today’s bomb threats.
The aircraft, operating flight number ROT226M, sent a squawk code of 7700 – general emergency – before landing safely in Bucharest. The threat was later confirmed to be unproven.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bomb threats against European flights ‘likely a coordinated campaign of disruption’, Ireland says – as it happened

articles.author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
articles.description:
Regulator’s initial ruling says algorithm ‘can be harmful’ and led young and vulnerable viewers ‘down rabbit holes they can’t easily escape’

TikTok has been charged by the European Commission with failing to protect users’ mental health by exposing them to a relentless stream of content that risks worsening eating disorders and anxiety in a case that strikes at its business model.
Issuing a preliminary ruling on Friday, the EU regulator said TikTok’s algorithm “can be harmful” and was leading young and vulnerable users “down rabbit holes they cannot easily escape from”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: EU charges TikTok with failing to protect users’ mental health

articles.author: Carlos Mureithi in Nairobi and agencies
articles.description:
Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families
The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.
The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children

articles.author: Andrew Messenger
articles.description:
Legal expert compares Trevor Hold’s failed defence to ‘tried and tested argument’ used by sovereign citizen movement

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Queensland leader of a group opposing the eradication of fire ants in Australia has been convicted of obstructing government officers, after a magistrate threw out his argument that the commonwealth-funded program is illegal.
Trevor Hold was fined $1,500 but a conviction was not recorded. Hold has described himself as an “ultrapreneur”, a mental health counsellor, an organic cattle farmer and the chief executive officer of the anti-program group the Australian Advocacy Group – and as self-employed.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Anti-fire ant eradication activist convicted after using legal arguments ‘similar to sovereign citizens’

articles.author: Benita Kolovos
articles.description:
Crashing into a shop awning ended the first outing of the Jess Express – but the opposition’s electoral momentum will be harder to stop

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

Jess Wilson has barely put a foot wrong since becoming Victorian Liberal leader a little under a year ago. That was until this week, which ended with her campaign bus reversing into a small business.
The bus was launched on Friday, a few days earlier than planned, in what appeared to be an effort to reset Wilson’s relationship with the Spring Street press pack.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Victorian Liberals’ campaign bus was supposed to be a reset. Instead it became the symbol of a rough week

articles.author: Tom Phillips in Rio de Janeiro
articles.description:
Far-right politician addresses Conservative Political Action Conference and makes unsubstantiated claims about election fraud
Flávio Bolsonaro, the far-right politician who lost Brazil’s presidential election last month, has insisted his defeat is not “the end for Brazil” as he battles to maintain political relevance after fleeing to the US.
Bolsonaro absconded early last week shortly after losing the 25 October election to the leftwing incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva by more than 4m votes.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro battles to remain relevant as he speaks at rightwing conference at Mar-a-Lago

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
articles.description:
Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result
The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.
Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted

articles.author: Jon Henley Europe correspondent
articles.description:
YouGov survey finds support for tree planting and emissions taxes but opposition to air travel and fuel levies

Europe live – latest updates

Europeans believe human-made climate change is real, a survey has shown, with most feeling action must be taken soon – as long as they do not have to sacrifice too much to achieve it.
The YouGov poll of six European countries showed between 69% (Germany) and 80% (France) of respondents believed the climate was changing, with few (1%-4%) denying it and 14-20% believing it was changing, but not as a result of human activity.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Most Europeans want action to tackle climate crisis but not at any cost, poll shows

articles.author: Ollie Lewis for MetDesk
articles.description:
Further south this week, severe thunderstorms affected midterms voting in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado
Despite the rapid descent into autumn in the northern hemisphere, parts of eastern North America have experienced an exceptionally late taste of summer in recent days. Temperatures approached 23C (73F) in New York and Boston, about 7-10C above what is expected in early November. The unseasonable warmth spilled into parts of eastern Canada, with temperatures exceeding 20C, about 10-15C above normal for the time of year. The balmy conditions were caused by an area of low pressure in the US midwest, dragging up exceptionally warm air from the Gulf of Mexico along its eastern flank. This area of low pressure will gradually drift eastwards, allowing temperatures to fall closer to the average.
Further south, severe thunderstorms have resulted in numerous flood warnings and evacuation warnings being issued this week across many states, with disruptive weather affecting polling stations in Florida, Oklahoma and Colorado. The powerful thunderstorms even resulted in a tornado touching down in Keyes, Oklahoma, forcing the relocation of a polling station. The tornado caused extensive damage, although no causalities have been reported. Officials across many states have requested federal funding assistance after the extreme weather resulted in widespread damage to homes and infrastructure.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Low pressure in US midwest brings unseasonable heat to New York and Boston

articles.author: Tiago Rogero South America correspondent
articles.description:
Santiago Peña’s rightwing administration had authorised Ueno Bank to drastically expand operations before collapse
Paraguay’s rightwing president, Santiago Peña, resigned on Thursday after a political and financial crisis collapsed the South American country’s banking system in recent days.
At the centre of the crisis is Ueno Bank, which in just a few years under Peña went from an obscure digital bank to one of the country’s largest lenders, claiming to have about 60% of Paraguay’s adult population as customers.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Paraguay’s president quits after millions of people’s savings frozen in bank crisis

articles.author: Jason Burke International security correspondent and agencies
articles.description:
President says he will make a decision on Sunday about who should try to build a government as Netanyahu rival is endorsed by 67 lawmakers 
Gadi Eisenkot, the main rival to Benjamin Netanyahu, secured endorsements on Thursday from a majority of lawmakers to try to form a government but Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, said it was still unclear who could break the deadlock and that he would decide on Sunday which of the two men should try first.
Of the Knesset’s 120 elected lawmakers, 67 had ​endorsed Eisenkot through several days of talks with Herzog, while 46 endorsed Netanyahu. Herzog said on Thursday that while the “results ‌of the consultations may appear clear”, there were “mutual vetoes between the blocs and within the blocs themselves” that make it difficult to say who has the ‌best shot to form a government.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Israel’s Herzog yet to decide on who should form government as Eisenkot secures significant backing

articles.author: Caroline Davies
articles.description:
Philippine official says there are ‘signs that point to Thomas Markle Jr’s involvement in crime’, but he’s not yet being treated as a suspect
The Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, has been named as a “person of interest” in the Philippine authorities’ inquiry into child sexual abuse image allegations made against her father, Thomas Markle Sr.
The country’s interior and local government secretary, Jonvic Remulla, told a press conference in Manila there were “signs that point that the son is involved in the crime as well”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Duchess of Sussex’s estranged half-brother ‘person of interest’ in child sexual abuse inquiry

articles.author: Owen Myers
articles.description:
New report finds that record label Ador stripped child protections from group’s contracts when they were minors
The superstar K-pop group NewJeans signed restrictive record label contracts that waived their right to “sleep, rest and free choice”.
A new report from the New York Times found that the contracts were signed when the members of the record-breaking girl group were aged 14 to 17.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: K-pop group NewJeans’s contract omitted rights to ‘sleep and free choice’ – report

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor
articles.description:
Dismissals follow Houthi victories and pressure from southern Yemenis for more power
The UN-recognised government of Yemen has shaken up its political and military leadership in an attempt to regain territory lost to the Houthis in September and lift the four-week siege of Taiz, the country’s third largest city.
A counteroffensive launched on 5 October and aimed at liberating the entire country from Houthi control has failed amid fighting that has left thousands dead on both sides. The air superiority of the government’s ally Saudi Arabia – which has had to fend off near-daily Houthi attacks on its airports and military bases – has not translated into progress on the ground.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Yemen’s president sacks ministers and officers in attempt to turn tide of war

articles.author: Danny Vincent in Hong Kong
articles.description:
Wong, 30, in prison since 2020, is only activist in Hong Kong prosecuted twice under national security law

Exclusive: Joshua Wong laments city’s fate from inside maximum security prison

The Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has been sentenced to 10 years in prison after earlier pleading guilty to “foreign collusion”, his second conviction under a national security law critics say has been used to silence political opposition in the city.
Wong, who rose to prominence as the teenage face of Hong Kong’s 2014 pro-democracy demonstrations, submitted his guilty plea in September. He had been accused of working with the exiled Hong Kong activist Nathan Law to urge foreign powers to impose sanctions, blockades or other hostile measures against China.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong sentenced to 10 years in prison in national security case

articles.author: Lisa O’Carroll Senior staff correspondent
articles.description:
Delivering net zero also at risk, say MPs as they call for centralised policy and funding for mines and diversification 
The UK is “dangerously” dependent on China for critical raw materials needed for the military, renewable energy infrastructure and AI, a parliamentary investigation has found.
MPs on the business select committee called for an urgent centralised policy and the creation of a “critical minerals finance facility” to help fund rare earth and other critical mineral mines, and deploy grants, equity and debt to accelerate a diversification programme.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK found to be ‘dangerously’ reliant on China for critical minerals needed for defence and AI

articles.author: Ben Doherty
articles.description:
Analysis by human rights organisation Global Echo shows 85 of 132 shipments over eight years contained more than US$5m of organic dates grown in settlements

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Millions of dollars of food grown in illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank has been shipped to Australia labelled as “produce of Israel”, a new analysis of trade data has shown.
The human rights legal organisation Global Echo has analysed commercial documents and official trade data from the Israeli government and the Australian Bureau of Statistics, showing at least US$5m (A$7.2m) of organic dates grown in illegal settlements across the West Bank have been shipped to Australia over the past eight years.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Food grown in illegal West Bank settlements being sold in Australia as ‘produce of Israel’

articles.author: Alice Speri
articles.description:
Even Trump seems to recognize that the relationship has become a political liability, and may never be the same

Q&A: Ask your questions about Democrats’ win in the midterms

Track live results from all 50 states

On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his brand of politics, even Donald Trump seemed to recognize that the US-Israel relationship had become a political liability.
Trump’s 11th-hour suggestion, on election morning, that he would cut military aid to Israel at the end of the year because, as he put it, “they don’t need it”, was condemned across the board – with pro-Palestinian advocates dismissing it as “desperate” and pro-Israel ones as “unserious”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The midterms were a thumping rebuke of the US-Israel relationship

articles.author: Sarah Johnson
articles.description:
Patient is ⁠in ​stable condition and will be transferred to a specialist ‘high consequence’ infectious disease unit
A British healthcare worker with Ebola is being evacuated from the Democratic Republic of the Congo to the UK for medical treatment, it has been confirmed.
“A British citizen currently in the DR Congo has tested positive for Ebola,” a spokesperson for the UK government said in a statement on Wednesday. “The UK has well-established procedures for dealing with cases like this, and those processes have been activated … The risk to the UK public from Ebola remains low.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: British healthcare worker with Ebola evacuated from DR Congo to UK

articles.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
articles.description:
Party expected to get less than a third of the vote amid frustration over water outages and power cuts
The African National Congress is on course for a bruising result in South Africa’s local elections on Wednesday as voters go to the polls amid deep discontent over water outages, power cuts and crumbling infrastructure.
The former liberation movement, which Nelson Mandela led to power in 1994 at the end of apartheid as South Africa’s first black president, is still likely to be the largest party. However, polls showed it getting less than a third of the vote, down from 45.6% at the last municipal elections in 2021 and 40.2% in 2024’s national elections.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ANC faces anger over poor services as South Africans vote in local elections

articles.author: Niha Masih
articles.description:
A previously unseen family archive offers a glimpse into the Indian Nobel prize winner’s artistic process and personal relationships in his final years

Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

It’s easy to run out of words to describe Rabindranath Tagore. The first non-European to win the Nobel prize in literature, Tagore was a Bengali poet, musician, novelist, philosopher, songwriter, painter, humanist and educator.
Born in 1861, Tagore left an indelible mark on the subcontinent’s literature, music, education and art. Among his enduring legacies are the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The private creative world of Rabindranath Tagore, the man Yeats called ‘greater than any of us’

articles.author: Patrick Greenfield, Elisângela Mendonça and Phoebe Weston and Spoorthy Raman
articles.description:
Guardian and Mongabay reveal approaches to officials and MPs on behalf of  Vantara zoo ahead of UK-chaired Cites meeting on endangered animal imports

British government ministers were told not to engage formally with Vantara, the controversial mega-zoo run by the Indian billionaire Anant Ambani, after lobbying efforts by the private animal sanctuary in the run-up to a UK-chaired meeting on the trade in endangered species, according to documents.
This week, the UK heads a 32-country committee meeting in Geneva of Cites, the United Nations body that regulates trade in endangered species. The meeting will examine how India has responded to compliance concerns about imports of endangered animals.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK ministers told not to engage formally with Indian mega-zoo after lobbying

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Led by Congress party, India’s opposition alliance channels anger over removal of 130 million names from voter roll
Thousands of opposition supporters have gathered in Delhi as protests against the Narendra Modi government continue to gather momentum.

articles.author: Jonathan Freedland
articles.description:
Yes, the Republicans suffered humiliating defeat. But the fact that a Trump presidency was even possible means something like it could happen again
He’s down, but not quite out. Barring divine or other intervention, Donald Trump will remain in the Oval Office for a further two years and 10 weeks. Or, as the White House put it in a plaintive social media post brimming with neediness: “PSA [Public Service Announcement]: Trump is still your president.” But that’s not the only reason why the global celebrations that greeted the Democratic tidal wave that swept Republicans out of even their deepest heartlands should be tempered, if only a tad.
Don’t get me wrong, the results of Tuesday’s midterm elections are cause for genuine international jubilation. The defeats of Trump allies in Serbia and Brazil were delicious appetisers, but this was the feast. No mere electoral setback in line with midterm tradition, this was a thorough repudiation of the second Trump presidency and of Trumpism. The 16% swing to Democrats in the popular vote for the House of Representatives was greater even than the 11.2% swing recorded in the Watergate midterms of November 1974, following the resignation in disgrace of Richard Nixon. Trump had worked hard for many months to undermine these elections, either by gerrymandering districts in his favour or preparing the ground for a later claim the vote was rigged, but to no avail: the democratic system proved too resilient, and the American public too determined to have their say. And have it they did, in a voice loud and clear.

But experts warned that although the health service was identifying more cases, it was still failing to meet timescale targets on diagnosis and treatment.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cancer diagnoses in England hit record high of more than 1,000 people a day

articles.author: Heather Stewart Economics editor
articles.description:
Base rate increases from 3.75% and Bank governor signals another rise in near future to combat rising inflation

Analysis: Interest rate rise in midst of cost of living crisis will leave many incredulous

The Bank of England has raised interest rates for the first time in three years and warned of another increase to combat inflationary pressure unleashed by the Iran war.
Eight members of the Bank’s monetary policy committee (MPC) voted for the rise, which takes the base rate from 3.75% to 4%. The ninth member, Catherine Mann, preferred a more dramatic half-point increase.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%, the first increase for more than three years

Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault

articles.description:
British College of Aesthetic Medicine launches checklist as part of ‘vet it before you get it’ campaign
Cosmetic tourism is often sold as a package of sun, sea and surgery, but experts have said travelling overseas for procedures can end in infections, disfigurement and death.
Nora Nugent, a consultant plastic surgeon and former president of the British Association of Aesthetic Plastic Surgeons, said travelling to countries such as Turkey for surgery came with myriad risks – and not just on the operating table.

articles.title: Beware ‘sun, sea and surgery’ cosmetic tourism packages, experts advise

articles.author: Emine Sinmaz
articles.description:
Actor and comedian, 51, found guilty of raping a woman and assaulting three others

Flashbulbs, lies and victim blaming: how Russell Brand’s trial unfolded

Russell Brand has been found guilty of raping a fan and sexually assaulting three other women, ending a years-long legal saga that has raised questions about how he was able to commit his crimes at the height of his fame.
Brand, 51, was described during his trial as a ruthless, calculated and manipulative sexual predator. He was convicted of raping a woman at his luxury London townhouse and of sexually assaulting women in front of his entourage at their workplaces, at a radio station and TV studio.

First rate rise for more than three years leaves millions facing rise in mortgage payments

The Bank of England has hiked interest rates by 0.25 percentage points, taking the base rate to 4%. It is the first rate rise for more than three years, leaving millions of households facing a sharp rise in mortgage payments.

articles.title: What does the UK interest rate rise mean for homeowners and savers?

articles.author: Phillip Inman
articles.description:
Bank’s decision goes contrary to analysis from Office for Budget Responsibility that predicts lower inflation and little impetus for wage growth

Bank of England raises interest rates to 4%

An interest rate rise by the Bank of England to 4% is a big call when households are suffering from a second cost of living crisis in four years.

articles.description:
In the Netherlands many felt the move, while welcome, was mishandled and exclusionary, mirroring past inequality
Andy Burnham’s pledge to seek a “structured dialogue” with former colonies to help shape Britain’s first formal state apology for slavery marks the UK’s first tentative step down a path the Netherlands set out on five years ago.
The prime minister’s attempts to initiate a historic shift alongside the royal family – whose customary expressions of “profound personal sorrow”, falling short of an apology, was repeated by King Charles this week – echo a process begun by the Dutch state in 2021.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: What can Britain learn from backlash to Dutch slavery apology?

articles.author: Aamna Mohdin
articles.description:
Debate has focused on cash payments, but advocates say reparatory justice must address much more than money
The debate in much of the British media over reparations has focused almost entirely on cash payments: how much Britain might owe for its role in transatlantic enslavement, who should pay and whether people today should be held responsible for the actions of those who came before them.
But some campaigners warn that this narrow focus overlooks the broader goals of the reparations movement.

articles.author: Karen McVeigh

Four-year study warns destabilised marine food webs could jeopardise food security by 2050
Warming seas around the UK and the wider north-east Atlantic could destabilise marine food webs, weaken ocean health and jeopardise food security by 2050, according to a four-year study.
Scientists who projected the impact of climate breakdown on four key groups of marine life crucial to maintaining ocean ecosystems in the region said their results challenged assumptions that in middle latitudes, such as the UK, marine biodiversity was likely to increase across the board.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Warming UK seas could ‘fundamentally reshape marine ecosystems’ – report

articles.author: Nicola Davis Science correspondent
articles.description:
Controversial theory that Verica, who incited Emperor Claudius’s AD43 landing, was a woman could put a new spin on British history if true
It was a moment that changed the course of British history: in AD43, Roman troops under the emperor Claudius landed in Kent. Now, an archaeologist has claimed the British ruler who persuaded Claudius to invade was not a king but a queen.
The controversial conclusion, made by Dr Miles Russell, the director of archaeological fieldwork at Bournemouth University, could throw new light on Britain’s history.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Historians say King Verica persuaded Rome to invade Britain. But could Verica actually have been a queen?

articles.author: Joe Pinner
articles.description:
Ministers urged to go further than proposed cut to 110 decibels to ease acute stress on birds and other animals
Campaigners are calling on the UK government to protect the welfare of wild animals by cutting the maximum noise level of fireworks sold to the public from 120 to 90 decibels.
The Center for Wild Animal Welfare (CWAW) has said lowering the limit to 90dB – which is about one-eighth of the loudness of 120dB – would help to protect millions of wild animals from acute stress by reducing the area over which a firework disturbs surrounding wildlife.

Speaking in Antigua and Barbuda, the king said the slave trade 'still casts a shadow over these islands and other members of our Commonwealth', but his remarks stopped short of an apology. King Charles addresses summit as campaigners intensify demands for apology for slavery

articles.author: Presented by Aditya Chakrabortty with Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal, produced by Frankie Tobi and Luke John Smith, executive producers Maz Ebtehaj, Kirsty Major and James Tindale.
articles.description:
What if someone told you the truth about the economy? For years, governments have tried spending more, spending less, cutting red tape, Brexit, levelling up – and still failed to increase growth per person in the UK. So what’s the lesson from the great British fairytale? On the latest episode of Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty, rebel economists Karel Williams and Sukhdev Johal explain why they believe praying for growth is a fool’s dream – and why it won’t improve your life
You can watch previous episodes of Radical Thinking here
  

  
Aditya’s suggested reading list for this episode:
 

 

 As we say in the podcast, I’ve championed the work of Karel and Sukhdev and their colleagues for many years in the Guardian, and some of my columns are a good introduction to their approach.
In our conversation we look at what life after growth looks like for towns and suburbs, and what it should look like. This report from south Wales in 2016 examines the present-day reality.
For a broader analysis of how the UK has become highly unequal and increasingly stagnant, try this.
As part of the Foundational Economy Collective, Williams and Johal put a lot of their analysis into freely available working papers. That circumvents the leisureliness and expense of academic publishing and gets their arguments in front of a wider public. A good example is this one on the cost of living crisis.
More recently, they’ve focused on the broken water system of England and Wales in a book called Murky Water: Challenging an Unsustainable System.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why politicians chasing economic growth is a lie | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty – podcast

articles.description:
Relatives recount distress and loneliness their loved ones went through in pandemic as a result of isolation policy
“At the time it felt like a devil’s bargain – it was horrible, but it was what [we thought] we had to do to keep people safe,” says Amy of the “devastating” and “terrifying” restrictions that led to her maternal grandparents being locked down in separate care homes during the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic.
Eva and Eric had been married for more than 60 years when her dementia and his increased frailty meant they needed separate residential support. When the first lockdown was announced in March 2020, however, it in effect cut them off from each other and their granddaughter, to whom they had been especially close after the early death of Amy’s mother.

Men allegedly impersonated voices and images of executives to convince employees to send large payments
Three foreign nationals were arrested and charged with using AI to allegedly impersonate corporate CEOs and attorneys to steal over $100m, according to an indictment that was newly unsealed by the US Department of Justice.
According to a press release from the United States attorney’s office for the southern district of New York, three men – Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan, and Guy Sheetrit – were arrested for using AI to alter and impersonate the voices and images of executives and attorneys at various companies in order to convince employees to send over large payments. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain over the summer, while Sheetrit was arrested in the United Kingdom in September. The alleged fraud took place between 2024 and 2026.

The best beauty Advent calendars of 2026 in the US

articles.author: Tom Regan
articles.description:
When our writer found himself among the hundreds on Oxford Street hoping to get their hands on early copies and collectibles, it was a heartwarming reminder of the shared experience of fandom
• The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
It is Thursday night and I am sat blurry-eyed and runny nosed outside the Argos on Oxford Street. Incredibly, I am far from alone. This is not some strange protest against the popular retailer. When the clock strikes midnight, the lavish 4K Switch 2 remake of beloved N64 classic The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time will be released, and I have joined a lengthy queue of about 500 fans desperate to snag early copies. There are similar events taking place across the world, from Melbourne to Mexico City; at key locations, Nintendo has senior executives waiting at the tills.
These days, of course, most video games are bought as digital copies that download straight to your PC or console on the day of release. You don’t even have to get out of bed to start playing. But in a bygone era, when we used to go to shops to buy games, midnight launches offered a space for likeminded enthusiasts to gather and celebrate their fandom. Every Call of Duty, Halo or Grand Theft Auto release would have fans queueing outside branches of Game or Electronics Boutique, many dressed as favourite characters.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has revived the midnight game launch – but was it worth the wait?

articles.author: Keza MacDonald
articles.description:
Titanium Court is a bizarre world of 8-bit fairies, Shakespeare and surprise songs – its magic lies in never knowing what on earth is going on
• Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here
Earlier this year, I was stuck in hospital for several days, fuzzy on pain medication and bored out of my mind, with nothing but a Steam Deck for company. In the middle of one of those long nights, unable to sleep, I played a game called Titanium Court. It’s a strange creation that looks like it was made for the ZX Spectrum and reads like a postmodern Shakespeare adaptation – a compelling mix of strategy game and match-3 where you rearrange battlefields by matching tiles, before sending tiny lo-fi fairy armies to their deaths.
At the end of this late-night run, I met a boss I’d defeated before – a comically hungry dragon – and the game asked if I would like to skip the boss fight and enjoy a musical performance instead. A game has never asked me this before. Of course, I accepted. And then, instead of the familiar tiled battlefield, I was looking at a pixellated singer-songwriter, who launched into an extremely long preamble about the mating habits of the Pacific salmon before saying, “This is a song for anyone else who ever got so horny they could die,” and launching into a soulful acoustic guitar number accompanied by crude images of leaping fish. I began to wonder if my meds were making me hallucinate.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Why the weirdest game of 2026 is also one of my favourites

articles.author: Keza MacDonald
articles.description:
Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo
This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains
It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time.
Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true

AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment
Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal.
That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI.
